This program reads data on fruit fly life span. Find more information in the [data dictionary][dd].

[dd]: https://github.com/pmean/data/blob/master/files/fruitfly.yaml

This code was written by Steve Simon on 2024-10-23 and is placed in the public domain.

## Datasets

-   fly: original data from fruitfly.txt
-   fly_1: created category levels
-   fly_2: re-order the categories in the variable cage
-   fly_3: log transformed life spans

## Models

-   m1: analysis of variance, longevity ~ cage
-   m2: linear regression, same variables
-   m3: analysis of variance, make no females the reference category
-   m4: analysis of variance on log transformed data
-   m5: Tukey post hoc confidence intervals for log transformed data

## Load the tidyverse library

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(broom)
library(tidyverse)
```

# --- Part 1

## List the variable names

```{r}
#| label: variable-list

fn <- "https://jse.amstat.org/datasets/fruitfly.dat.txt"
vlist <- c(
  "id",
  "partners",
  "type",
  "longevity",
  "thorax",
  "sleep")
```

#### Comments on the code

When a dataset does not have variables on the first line, you need to specify them in the code.

## Read the data and view a brief summary

```{r}
#| label: read

fly <- read_table(
  "../data/fruitfly.txt",
  col_types="nnnnnn",
  col_names=vlist)
glimpse(fly)
```

#### Comments on the code

The read_table function is part of the readr library, which is included when you specify the tidyverse library. You can use this function when you have one or more blanks or tabls between each data value.

## Create cage groups

```{r}
#| label: cage

fly |>
  mutate(cage=case_when(
    fly$partners==0 & fly$type==9 ~ "No females",
    fly$partners==1 & fly$type==0 ~ "One pregnant female",
    fly$partners==1 & fly$type==1 ~ "One virgin female",
    fly$partners==8 & fly$type==0 ~ "Eight pregnant females",
    fly$partners==8 & fly$type==1 ~ "Eight virgin females")) -> fly_1
```

#### Comments on the code

The case_when function is part of the dplyr library, which is included when you specify the tidyverse library. This function evaluates a series of tests (listed on the left side of the tilde) and assigns the particular value to the first test that evaluates to TRUE. If no test evaluates to TRUE, the case_when function assigns a missing value.

## Calculate descriptive statistics

```{r}
#| label: longevity-means

fly_1 |>
  group_by(cage) |>
  summarize(
    longevity_mn=mean(longevity),
    longevity_sd=sd(longevity),
    n=n())
```

#### Interpretation of the output

The mean lifespan is 39 days for the "Eight virgin females" category, which is much lower than the other means. The means lifespan is 57 days for the "One virgin female" category and this is slightly lower than the remained three categories. The standard deviations are reasonably small and more or less consistent across all groups.

## Draw boxplot

```{r}
#| label: longevity-boxplot
#| fig.width: 6
#| fig.height: 2.5

fly_1 |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(longevity, cage) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    caption="Simon, 2024-10-23",
    x="Lifespan (days)",
    y="Cage residents")
```

#### Interpretation of the output

The boxplot shows a roughly normal distribution with no outliers.

## One factor analysis of variance for longevity

```{r}
#| label: longevity-one-factor-anova

m1 <- aov(longevity ~ cage, data=fly_1)
tidy(m1)
```

#### Interpretation of the output

The F-ratio is large and the p-value is small. Conclude that there is a 
difference among some or all of the population mean lifespans.

## Linear model for longevity, 1

```{r}
#| label: longevity-lm-1

m2 <- lm(longevity ~ cage, data=fly_1)
anova(m2)
```

#### Interpretation of the output

You can use linear regression to reach the same conclusion. The sums of squares,
degrees of freedom, F-ratio, and p-value all match.

## Linear model for longevity, 2

```{r}
#| label: longevity-lm-2

tidy(m2)
```

#### Comments on the code

The test statistics and p-values listed here do not make any adjustments for multiple comparisons. Some researchers think this is fine. Others prefer that you use the Tukey post hoc comparisons, which insures that the overall Type I error rate is less than 0.05.

#### Interpretation of the output

The linear model creates indicator variable for four out of the five category
levels. The reference category is "Eight pregnant females" which is the first category level in alphabetical order. 

The intercept, 63 days, is the estimated average life span in days for the "Eight pregnant females" category.

The first slope is -25. The estimated average life span decreases by 25 days when you switch from the "Eight pregnant females" category to the "Eight virgin females" category.

The second slope is 0.2. The estimated average life span increases by 0.2 days when you switch from the "Eight pregnant females" category to the "No females" category.

The third slope is 1.4. The estimated average life span increases by 1.4 days when you switch from the "Eight pregnant females" category to the "One pregnant female" category.

The fourth slope is -6.6. The estimated average life span decreases by 6.6 days when you switch from the "Eight pregnant females" category to the "One virgin female" category.

## Re-order cage groups, 1

```{r}
#| label: re-order-1
new_order <- c(
  "No females",
  "One pregnant female",
  "Eight pregnant females",
  "One virgin female",
  "Eight virgin females")

fly_1 |>
  mutate(cage=factor(cage, levels=new_order)) -> fly_2
```

#### Comments on the code

The [factor function][ref-factor], part of base R, creates a new variable with number codes and labels. The order of labels is designated by the levels argument.

In this example, the code creates a reference category of "no females" instead of the default reference category based on alphabetical order.

[ref-factor]: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/base/html/factor.html

## Re-order cage groups, 2

```{r}
#| label: re-order-2

m3 <- lm(longevity ~ cage, data=fly_2)
tidy(m3)
```

#### Interpretation of the output

The estimated average life span is 64 days for the cage with no females. The cages with one and eight pregnant females change only slightly: one day or less on average. The cage with one virgin female has 6.8 days less in life span on average and the cage with eight virgin females has 25 fewer days in average life span.

Do not interpret the p-values because they are not adjusted for multiple comparisons.

## Tukey post-hoc test

```{r}
m4 <- aov(longevity ~ cage, data=fly_2)
TukeyHSD(m4)
```

#### Interpretation of the output

There are ten possible comparisons among the five groups. Six of the confidence intervals contain zero. This indicates that there is no statistically significant difference between 

-   one pregnant female and no females
-   eight pregnant females and no females
-   eight pregnant females and one pregnant female
-   one virgin female and no females
-   one virgin female and one pregnant female
-   one virgin female and eight pregnant females

There is a statistically significant decrease in average life span for

-   eight virgin females compared to no females
-   eight virgin females compared to one pregnant female
-   eight virgin females compared to eight pregnant females
-   eight virgin females compared to one virgin female

# --- Part 2

## Log transformation, 1

```{r}
#| label: log-longevity-anova-1

fly_2 |>
  mutate(log_longevity=log10(longevity)) -> fly_3

m4 <- aov(log_longevity ~ cage, data=fly_3)
tidy(m4)
```

#### Interpretation of the output

Although there are no problems with heterogeneity or non-normality, here is an 
illustration of how to use a log transformation with analysis of variance.

The F-ratio is large and the p-value is small. You can conclude that at least two of the population mean log life spans differ from one another.

You can use the Tukey post hoc test examine whether the intervals include or exclude the value of zero, but interpretation using log-days as the unit of measurement is tricky.

## Log transformation, 2

```{r}
#| label: log-longevity-anova-2

m4 |>
  TukeyHSD() |>
  tidy() -> m5

m5 |> 
  select(contrast, estimate, conf.low, conf.high) |>
  mutate(estimate=10^estimate) |>
  mutate(conf.low=10^conf.low) |>
  mutate(conf.high=10^conf.high)
```

#### Comments on the code

It is better to transform these results back to the original scale of measurement before interpreting the confidence intervals.

#### Interpretation of the output

When you back-transform after a log transformation, the confidence intervals are confidence intervals for a ratio of means. If the confidence interval includes the value of 1, there is no statistically significant difference between the two groups.

In this example, there are four statistically significant differences, all involving the cage with eight virgin females. The fruitflies with eight virgin females have a life span that 40% shorter on average frutiflies with no females. The relevant computation is 100*(1-0.5961729). This ratio is statistically significant meaning that it is too large to be accounted for by sampling error. The confidence interval for the ratio is 0.48 to 0.75. Even after allowing for sampling error, the life span is at least 25% shorter and possibly as much as 52% shorter.

The interpretations comparing the average life span of the flies with eight virgin females to the other cages (one virgin female, one pregnant female, eight pregnant females). The average life span of flies with eight virgin females is 42% shorter than flies with one pregnant female, 40% shorter than flies with pregnant females, and 33% shorter than flies with one virgin female. All of these changes are statistically significant.

There are no statistically significant difference in average life spans among the files with no females, one pregnant female, eight pregnant females, and one virgin female. For example, the ratio of average longevity comparing one pregnant female to no females is 1.02, or 2% larger. The confidence interval ranges from 0.82 or 18% smaller to 1.28 or 28% larger. There is no statistically significant change in longevity between fruitflies caged alone and fruitflies caged with one pregnant female.

Always provide an interpretation, but you should not have to interpret every statistic that your computer spits out. Interpreting everything leads to turgid prose. This is especially true for the Tukey post hoc confidence intervals when you have a large number of categories. If you say, this interval means this and this interval means this and this interval means this, and so on, your writing will be boring at best and confusing at worst. Use your judgement on this, of course, but focusing on a limited number of intervals, such as those compared to the "best" group or those compared to the current standard of treatment or those that show statistical significance may make sense.

# --- Part 3

## Kruskal-Wallis test

```{r}
#| label: kw

kruskal.test(longevity ~ cage, data=fly_2)
```

#### Comments on the code

The [kruskal.test function][ref-kruskal], part of base R, produces the Kruskal-Wallis test, non-parametric alternative to one factor analysis of variance.

[ref-kruskal]: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/kruskal.test.html

#### Interpretation of the output

It may not be needed with this particular dataset, but this is an illustration
of how to use the Kruskal-Wallis test. 

The chi-squared statistic is much larger than its degrees of freedom and the p-value is small, so you should reject the null hypothesis and conclude that there is a difference between at least two of the five population means.

## Save important files for later use

```{r}
#| label: save

save(
  fly,
  fly_1,
  fly_2,
  fly_3,
  file="../data/fruitfly.RData")
```
